book.title: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk

pages.title: The First Linguistic Study of Turkic
pages.content:
Dîvânü lugāti’t-Türk, which means ‘Dictionary of Turkic Dialects (Lehçe)’, is the first linguistic study of the Turkic language. It was written by Mahmud Kashgari in 11th-century Karakhanid (Karahanlı) Turkish. A dialect is a regional form of a language with its own special vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation. So, as the title of the book shows, this study includes the speech patterns, vocabulary, and grammar rules of different Turkic tribes.

Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk was prepared as a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic. It aimed to teach the Turkic language to Arabs and prove that it is just as rich as Arabic. The comprehensive content of the work shows that Mahmud Kashgari had an advanced knowledge of both Arabic and Persian. In addition, he was very knowledgeable about the dictionaries written in these languages.

pages.title: Who Was Mahmud Kashgari?
pages.content:
Mahmud Kashgari was born in 1008 and died in 1105. It is generally believed that he was born in Barsgan, which is in Kyrgyzstan today, and died in Kashgar (Kaşgar). Today, Kashgar is located in China’s Sincan Uyghur Autonomous Region. This area is a historical Turkish homeland also widely known as East Turkestan (Doğu Türkistan).

Kashgari says that he belongs to a noble family, and his ancestor was Nasr Ilig Khan, the famous Karakhanid ruler who conquered Transoxiana (Maveraünnehir) and Bukhara. He also says he is one of the Turks who knows the language best, one of the clearest speakers, one of the wisest, and one of the best spear throwers.

pages.title: Writing the Dîvân
pages.content: Mahmud Kashgari began writing Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk in 1072 and, after improving it several times and making new additions, completed it in 1074. After that, he presented his work to the Abbasid Caliph (Abbasi Halifesi) Muktedî-Biemrillâh in Baghdad in 1077. The work contains about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms. It also includes the oldest examples of Turkic poetry, grammar rules of the Turkic language, many place names, personal names, various traditions, beliefs, and legends from the Turkic world of that time. In addition, it has information and practices related to nearly every aspect of life. For this reason, the work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.

pages.title: Words About the Turks
pages.content:
In his work, Kashgari states that Allah gave the Turks their name and placed them in the highest part of the world, where the air is the cleanest. He writes down that Allah called the Turks His own army. He then describes many good qualities of the Turks, such as beauty, bright faces, good manners, modesty, bravery, and respect for elders. He also records the following hadith (hadis) on the same subject. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) says, “Learn the Turkish language! This is because the Turks will have a long-lasting kingdom.”

Owing to this belief and confidence, he started his journey and began to visit all Turkic countries. Mahmud of Kashgar left his home in 1057. In the next ten or fifteen years, until he arrived in Baghdad, he traveled from one Turkic tribe to another. During this time, he collected the material that he needed for his work. He says that he studied the lands of the Turks and learned the dialects of the Turks, Turkmen, Oghuz (Oğuz), Chigil (Çiğil), Yagma (Yağma), and Kyrgyz (Kırgız). He also adds that he knew the language of every tribe perfectly.

pages.title: The Oghuz and the Caliph
pages.content:
The Oghuz are the Turkic tribe that gets the most attention in the book. At that time, the Oghuz were the most powerful tribe in the western part of the Turkic world, close to the Arab and Persian regions. The information Kashgari provides about them is not only about their language. The book also offers very useful explanations about how their tribes were organized. He writes the names of twenty-two of the twenty-four Oghuz tribes.

The reason why Kashgari drew so much attention to this tribe is probably that the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe, were very strong and protected the Abbasids, the center of the Islamic world. It is very important that a book with this information was finished in Baghdad, the capital city of the Abbasids, and given to the caliph. It is likely that Kashgari was aware of the Turks’ political power and of the fact that the Turks protected the caliph. The three great Turkic states of the time were the Karakhanids (Karahanlılar), the Ghaznavids (Gazneliler), and the Seljuks (Selçuklular).

pages.title: The Importance of the Map
pages.content:
Besides all this language material, the book also includes a map of the Turkic world of his time. Because of this map, which is considered the oldest document made from a Turkic geographical perspective, Kashgari is known as the first Turkic cartographer.

Mahmud of Kashgar says that Allah placed the Turks on the highest mountains, the center of the world, so they could rule the earth and control the whole world. It is likely that he made his map to reflect this belief. On the map, Turkestan, the homeland of the Turks, is in the center of the world. Also, the city of Balasagun, which is in modern-day Kyrgyzstan, is placed right in the heart of it. In fact, Balasagun was on a very busy part of the Silk Road. He placed all other countries, cities, and mountains according to this center. The map has a colorful, circular design. It shows mountains in red, seas in green, rivers in blue, and sandy areas in yellow. It also shows the nations that had relations with the Turks.

Based on modern geography, the places on Mahmud of Kashgar’s world map go as far west as the Russian border and the Idil (Volga) River. In the south, they go from the Egyptian border to Ethiopia and India, and they reach China and Japan in the east. Interestingly, Japan is called ‘Jabarqa’ on the map, while China is shown as ‘the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc.’

With today’s knowledge, the map in Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first world map that shows Japan. The second map to show Japan like Kashgari’s map was made about four hundred years after his book.

pages.title: The Story of the Calendar
pages.content:
The book also includes information about the ancient calendar used by the Turks. In the dictionary section, Kashgari explains the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar in detail. He describes the origin of this calendar and its importance in Turkish daily life. According to the text, the Turks made a twelve-year system and gave the names of twelve different animals to the years. They used this method to record their children’s ages, war dates, and other historical events. The historical background of this calendar is explained below:

One of the Turkic khans (a title used for Turkish rulers) wanted to learn the date of an old war from the past. However, the people around him did not agree on the correct date. Therefore, the khan called a kurultay, which was a national meeting, to talk with his people.

The khan said: “If we make a mistake about this date, the people after us will also make a mistake. To prevent this, let us make a system based on the twelve stars in the sky and the twelve months. We should give a name to each year. In this way, we can determine the time by counting these years. This system will be a useful record for everyone.” The people agreed with the khan’s idea. They decided to choose the names for the years in this way:

The khan went out to hunt and ordered his people to drive the wild animals toward a large river in the Ili Valley (İli Vadisi). The Ili Valley is a historically and geographically significant region located in the northern part of East Turkestan, stretching across the border into Kazakhstan (Kazakistan). The people chased them toward the river. In the end, only twelve animals could cross the river. The first animal to cross was the rat, so the first year was named after it. Then, the names of the other animals were given to the following years in the exact order they crossed. Therefore, the calendar starts with the Year of the Rat. After the rat, the years in the calendar follow the order of the animals that crossed the river successfully:

pages.title: What Each Year Means
pages.content:
In the Twelve-Animal Turkic Calendar, some years are seen as good and successful, while others are seen as difficult. For this reason, the Turks have a belief about each year and find specific meanings in it. For example, if it is the Year of the Ox, they believe that wars will increase because the ox is an animal that fights with its horns. When the Year of the Rooster begins, food becomes easy to find, but problems grow among people. This is because the rooster eats grain and always searches for food in waste heaps. When the Year of the Snake and the Year of the Crocodile start, there is plenty of rain and the land becomes rich because the natural home of these animals is water. Finally, when the Year of the Pig begins, cold weather, snow, and confusion increase. In this way, the Turks make different predictions for each year.

History shows that the Turks used this calendar for a very long time. For example, historical events are described according to the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar on the Orkhon Monuments, which were made in the years 725, 731, and 732. The months on the monuments are numbered. For example, the first month is written as birinç ay and the fifth month is written as bişinç ay. This was hundreds of years before Kashgari wrote his Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk.

According to the information from Kashgari, the Twelve-Animal Turkic calendar starts on March 21 in the modern calendar. Nowruz, which the Turks have celebrated since ancient times, is the first day of the new year in this calendar. Today, Turks and different communities in the Turkic world and the surrounding regions still continue to celebrate Nowruz (Nevruz) as a traditional holiday.

pages.title: Founder of Turkic Studies
pages.content:
Mahmud of Kashgar is regarded as the founder of Turkic studies. He was a very well-educated linguist. UNESCO included the 950th Anniversary of his famous work, Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk, in its 2024 celebration program. This idea was suggested by Turkey and supported by Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

Today, the only copy of Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk that still exists is in the Millet Library in Istanbul.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the language of the whole book.

exercises.title: Notice: How Sure Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: stated as fact, or presented as possible or believed?
exercises.question: How sure is the writer?

items: Mahmud Kashgari was born in 1008 and died in 1105.
The work contains about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms.
It is generally believed that he was born in Barsgan.
It is likely that he made his map to reflect this belief.

Stated as fact: Mahmud Kashgari was born in 1008 and died in 1105.
The work contains about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms.
Possible or believed: It is generally believed that he was born in Barsgan.
It is likely that he made his map to reflect this belief.

exercises.explanation: The writer uses It is generally believed and It is likely that when something is not completely certain (Chapters 2 and 7).

feedback.correct: Good. You noticed the writer’s certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Look for believed and likely.

exercises.title: Notice: Who or Which?
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences. Then choose the correct one.
exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Nasr Ilig Khan was the Karakhanid ruler who conquered Bukhara.
Nasr Ilig Khan was the Karakhanid ruler which conquered Bukhara.
Nasr Ilig Khan was the Karakhanid ruler where conquered Bukhara.
exercises.explanation: Use who for people and which for things.

feedback.incorrect: Is Nasr Ilig Khan a person or a thing?

exercises.title: Notice: After + -ing
exercises.instructions: Read the statement. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: In “After improving it several times, he completed it”, improving happened first.
exercises.explanation: “After + -ing” shows the earlier action.

feedback.incorrect: Which action came first?

exercises.title: Build: Linking Ideas
exercises.instructions: Fill each gap from the word bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: How does the book link ideas?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The khan wanted to learn the date of an old war. [blank], the people did not agree. [blank], he called a kurultay. Some years are seen as good, [blank] others are seen as difficult.
exercises.explanation: “However” shows a contrast between sentences. “Therefore” gives a result. “While” contrasts two parts of one sentence.

feedback.incorrect: Is it a contrast or a result?

exercises.title: Build: Choose the Form
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence.
exercises.question: Which form fits?

formChoices.sentence: If we make a mistake, the people after us [choice] also make a mistake.
The status of Arabic made Kashgari [choice] his own language.
He is one of the best spear [choice].

exercises.explanation: Use will in the first conditional, the base verb after make + person, and a plural noun after one of the.

feedback.incorrect: Check the conditional, make and one of the.

exercises.title: Build: Correct the Sentences
exercises.instructions: Find the mistake and choose the correct form.
exercises.question: Which form is correct?

errorItems.sentence: Owing to he believed in Turkish, he started his journey.
The map goes as far west than the Russian border.
The idea was suggested from Turkey.

exercises.explanation: “Owing to” needs a noun; use “because” before a clause. We say “as far west as”. The passive uses “by”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Because he believed, as, by.
feedback.incorrect: Check owing to, as … as and the passive.

exercises.title: Build: Say It Another Way
exercises.instructions: Complete the new sentence. Keep the same meaning.
exercises.question: How else can we say it?

transformItems.source: Most people think that he was born in Barsgan.
transformItems.frame: It is generally [blank] that he was born in Barsgan.

transformItems.source: People think of Kashgari as the founder of Turkic studies.
transformItems.frame: Kashgari is [blank] as the founder of Turkic studies.

transformItems.source: He started his journey because of this belief.
transformItems.frame: He started his journey owing [blank] this belief.

exercises.explanation: Use It is generally believed, be regarded as and owing to to sound more formal.

feedback.incorrect: Use believed, regarded and to.

exercises.title: Use: A New Context
exercises.instructions: Read about a modern dictionary project. Fill each gap from the word bank.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s language in a new text?
exercises.fillBlanksText: A group of students started a project to record the [blank] of their region. They visited older people and collected words [blank] to farming and food. Their teacher had an [blank] knowledge of Turkish. It is [blank] that their small dictionary will help future students.
exercises.explanation: Dialect, related to, advanced and It is likely that come from the book. Here they describe a modern school project.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new text.
feedback.incorrect: Read the words around each gap.

exercises.title: Use: Check a Short Report
exercises.instructions: A student wrote about a museum visit. Find and correct each mistake.
exercises.question: What should the student change?

errorItems.sentence: The museum was opened from the city in 1990.
It has one of the oldest map in Türkiye.
The guide made us to look at the colors carefully.

exercises.explanation: Use “by” in the passive, a plural noun after “one of the”, and the base verb after “make + person”.

feedback.incorrect: Check the passive, one of the and make.

exercises.title: Use: A Book That Keeps a Culture Alive
exercises.instructions: Write six to eight sentences about a book or record that keeps a culture alive.
exercises.question: What does it contain, and why is it important?
exercises.explanation: Example: “My grandmother’s recipe notebook was written by her mother in the 1960s. It contains more than one hundred recipes from our region. Some of the dishes are not cooked anymore in our town. The notebook also includes short notes about weddings and holidays. It is regarded as a treasure in our family. It is likely that without it, many of these dishes would be forgotten. I want to type it and share it with my cousins.”

feedback.correct: Check: a passive, contains, is regarded as and It is likely that.

discussionPrompts.question: Name the book or record and who made it.
Say what it contains.
Say why it is important, with a careful explanation.
discussionPrompts.example: It is likely that without it, …
